effects.contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; jazz factors compared to the MUSIC factors via attribute column-vector correlations
effects.description: Individual differences in music preferences are described by five MUSIC dimensions (Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, Contemporary) defined by particular auditory and psychological attributes rather than by genre.
effects.citation_sentence: Previous research suggests that the MUSIC factors are defined and differentiated by certain musical attributes that account for significant proportions of variance in preferences over and above genre classification (Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin, 2011). ... The strongest test, therefore, of this hypothesis would be if the five MUSIC factors could be replicated solely using musical excerpts from a single genre.
effects.evidence: Study 2 Results/Summary: "The five-factor solution that emerged in the Internet sample was highly consistent with our expectations and clearly resembled the MUSIC model." ... "The present results supported our hypothesis and revealed five jazz-preference factors." But: "at least four of the five jazz-preference factors clearly resemble the MUSIC factors"; Sophisticated psychological convergence = -.40 (Table 4).
effects.notes: Self-replication. The original did not test within-genre structure, so this extends the five-factor claim to a single genre with new jazz stimuli: close extension, with conceptual as a possible alternative. The citation sentence was revised in pass 2 to the Study 2 introduction sentence that names Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin (2011), the same sentence luna56 used. Result: the authors say their hypothesis was supported and five factors emerged. However, the Sophisticated jazz factor 'showed no convergence on the psychological attributes' (r = -.40), so a second coder could call this inconclusive (partial support). The Internet and undergraduate samples are one entry: they are two samples of one study, the undergraduate sample checks the reliability of the same structure (congruence .96, .94, .97, .68, .94), and the attribute analysis pools them.

effects.original_authors: Rentfrow, Peter J.; Goldberg, Lewis R.; Levitin, Daniel J.
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.replication_study: Study 3 (rock excerpts; Facebook sample N = 1,786 and University of Texas undergraduate sample N = 374)
effects.outcome: Factor structure of liking ratings for rock-only excerpts (whether five MUSIC-like factors emerge) and convergence of their attribute profiles with the mixed-genre and jazz MUSIC factors
effects.contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; rock factors compared to the MUSIC factors via attribute column-vector correlations
effects.description: Individual differences in music preferences are described by five MUSIC dimensions (Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, Contemporary) defined by particular auditory and psychological attributes rather than by genre.
effects.citation_sentence: Studies 2 and 3 were designed to examine the structure of preferences for pieces of music within genres. Specifically, preferences for various jazz musical pieces were assessed in Study 2 and preferences for various rock pieces were assessed in Study 3. [General Discussion:] Using multiple pieces of music, methods, and samples, three studies were conducted to test the replicability of the five-dimensional music-preference model ... Taken together, these results provide almost complete replication of the MUSIC model
effects.evidence: Study 3 Summary: "The results from this study once again support the hypothesis ... results from the factor analyses revealed five rock-preference factors ... those factors were defined by attributes that resembled the preference models observed in Studies 1 and 2." Rock vs mixed-genre psychological column-vector correlations = .93, .70, .91, .97, and .25 (M, U, S, I, C).
effects.notes: Self-replication that extends the five-factor claim to rock-only stimuli: close extension, with conceptual as a possible alternative. Study 3's own section does not cite Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin (2011) by name; it calls itself 'a further test of the hypothesis that the MUSIC model reflects ...' (the Study 2 hypothesis attributed to that paper). The authors call the result support, but a second coder could call it inconclusive: (1) the Contemporary factor converged only weakly with the mixed-genre factor on psychological attributes (.25); (2) convergence with the jazz factors was lower (psychological S = -.53, C = -.19); (3) parallel analysis suggested six factors in the Internet sample. The Internet and undergraduate samples are one entry (congruence .86, .98, .92, .98, .85), as in Study 2. General Discussion: 28 of 35 attribute comparisons were significantly similar, and the authors call the results an 'almost complete replication of the MUSIC model'.
